What AI developers could learn from Charles Bukowski? (galjot.si)

This is why there is growing anti-AI sentiment. It is always extractive. You can never just enjoy a poem, you need to use it. You need to extract its value for shareholders. Get a life.


Is this a comment toward the author?

Surely the irony isn't lost upon you that they literally are advocating for getting a life.


Creatives have always found inspiration from what they consume (AI has nothing to do with it). My partner writes, and eventually gets to the point where she has to take a break from plotting and writing and watch tv shows or read books. When she says she needs to refill her well, I know she's about to want to watch tv shows again for a little bit.

I design games. I can't even count the number of times something someone said, or a game I've played or watched a review of, has sparked an idea for new game, especially a board game (which most of the time doesn't work out once it gets in front of players, but that's okay). It's probably been over a hundred times by now.

People love highlighting quotes from poems and stories that they find inspirational for their own lives somehow. You want to know how I know? Kindle used to tell me, with saying how many other people highlighted a specific passage (it might still do that, but I mostly listen to audiobooks right now, so of course I won't see them). Also social media is flooded with people sharing quotes from various books or poems or sayings from people.

That's all this is.

But because it's said by someone who works with A.I. and thus is thinking about the quote with that frame of reference, you had to twist it into some anti-A.I. sentiment, implying that he's doing something perverted or not normal by daring to find inspiration in a quote.


Bukowski was a fan on new technology even towards the end of his life:

> “Yes, you have a strange project: electronic books. It might be the future as more and more people find that the computer is such a magic thing: time-saver, charmer, energizer.”

No one can say what he would have thought of AI for sure but I think he would have appreciated ability to reduce drudgery on this thoughts on factotum[1] work.

1. Why yes, that is a cheesy reference to his book of the same name. ;)


> On Christmas Day, 1990, Charles Bukowski received a Macintosh IIsi computer and a laser printer from his wife, Linda. The computer utilized the 6.0.7 operating system and was installed with the MacWrite II word processing program. By January 18 of the next year, the computer was up and running and so, after a brief period of fumbling and stumbling, was Bukowski. His output of poems doubled in 1991.

Charles Bukowski, William Burroughs, and the Computer - https://realitystudio.org/bibliographic-bunker/charles-bukow...


This cracked me up. I only used ~~one~~ two of his poems and enjoyed most of the others. Betting on the Muse was $2.09 on Amazon, which is a good ROI, I think.


Bukowski worked as a mailman. I had that job too. It was an awesome job. I got through like 9 hours of audiobooks a day.

Only issue was nobody sends mail anymore -- the elderly, Christmas and spam -- so when there was no mail, you'd work an hour and then you'd only get paid one hour. So most people were students, or their spouse did the heavy lifting.

Other than the pay, it was a great job though. I worked in snowstorms (and regular storms!) and in >37C (~100F) -- I got a big sombrero which looked a bit silly but did the job.

Then I'd go home and work on genetic algorithms. And then when the pay arrived at the end of the month -- 800 Euros (909 American), I had to wonder if I wasn't doing it backwards -- I should be getting paid to work on genetic algorithms all day, and then at the end of the day I should run up and down staircases for several hours for free.


All writing is difficult. The most you can hope for is a day when it goes reasonably easily. plumbers don't get plumbers block, and doctors don't get doctors block; why should writers be the only profession that gives a special name to the difficulty of working and then expects sympathy for it?

—Philip Pullman


> "Go into yourself. Find out the reason that commands you to write; see whether it has spread its roots into the very depths of your heart; confess to yourself whether you would have to die if you were forbidden to write.

> This most of all: ask yourself in the most silent hour of your night: Must I write? Dig into 1 yourself for a deep answer. And if this answer rings out in assent, if you meet this solemn question with a strong, simple 'I must,' then build your life in accordance with this necessity..."

--Rainer Maria Rilke

Meanwhile Rilke gives no sympathy saying don't write because it is easy, hard, or your job, write because your existence demands it.

I've found writing software for domains is agnostic; there isn't much difference between make a CRM for Real Estate or ERP for car mechanic shops. It is curious that I know one person who is as passionate about the event ticket industry as Rilke is about writing -- they would rather die than not scalp tickets.

I would have to read `Letters to a Young Poet again`. Rilke addresses the difference between being an artist (Rilke a Poet apprenticed under Rodin to learn not sculpture but guidance to live as an artist) and entering a structured profession.


Beautiful.

Charles Bukowski said something similar…

> /…/ no baby, if you’re going to create you’re going to create whether you work 16 hours a day in a coal mine or you’re going to create in a small room with 3 children while you’re on welfare, you’re going to create with part of your mind and your body blown away, you’re going to create blind crippled demented, you’re going to create with a cat crawling up your back while the whole city trembles in earthquake, bombardment, flood and fire. baby, air and light and time and space have nothing to do with it and don’t create anything except maybe a longer life to find new excuses for.


I said last year, "if I'd known I was going to be homeless for this long, I would have just kept working on my game the whole time."

It seemed logical, at the time, to postpone such frivolous affairs until life was more orderly. But it sure didn't help speed things along.

On another note, I have also heard it said that one must suffer for one's art, but I haven't found much correlation personally between suffering and art... except perhaps to the degree that JavaScript is involved!


A while back I started a substack and diligently posted every day, for about a month.

The first few posts had some actual substance (a kind of backlog I suppose), but eventually I realized that I was just posting because I had decided to post and I didn't actually have anything left to say.

So I just stopped posting. I guess it'll probably be a few more years until the next one :)

(Gosh, just imagine if YouTube operated on this principle...)


“. . .a lonely room, with a cup of coffee, facing a blank piece of paper.”

Wouk elaborated on that predicament. He said that writer William Faulkner was asked, ‘Mr. Faulkner, do you write on inspiration or do you write on a schedule?’ Faulkner replied. ‘Well, of course I write on inspiration. Fortunately, it strikes every morning at a quarter past nine.’

https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/30/inspire-nine/


I'm not a plumber, but I'm in the trades, and we absolutely get a "block", but we grind through it.


>Why aren't we spending more time on the beach.

I think this comes down to getting paid per effort invested (measured in time) vs getting paid for the result.

If the average person were self-employed and received income proportional to their economic output, then they would be rewarded for working faster, instead of punished.

If they increased their productivity, by means of technology, they could then simply choose to work fewer hours.[0]

I noticed this before AI. If someone does the same job twice as fast, do they deserve half as much compensation?

What if they find a way to automate an entire process? What if they replace months of "manual labor" (tedious refactoring) with a perl script that produces the same result, deterministically?

A friend of mine once automated a woman's entire job away. He thought he was doing her a favour, freeing her from the drudgery, so she could focus on the other parts of the job. She wasn't so happy, when she revealed to him, that there weren't any.

---

[0] But most people aren't in such a position, and have to stay the required number of hours regardless of how much has been achieved. And I'm increasingly hearing reports of some kind of burnout resulting from being expected to keep up with machines that work a thousand times faster than you.

And that's now... Just wait until the big providers switch to Cerebras in a week or two!

(Though at that token speed, the silver lining is the work becomes interactive again, so if you use it correctly, your mental model does not desynchronize from the codebase, i.e. you don't need to spend extra time later catching up. But that deserves its own thread, I think :)


Your friend could have still done the woman a favor, if he shared the automation with her privately, instead of with their employer.

Doing things like this for yourself is how you make automation work for you instead of against you. Then you can take some of your extra time to automate even more. Or, if you're a dev, to clean up code so it's easier to work on later, or to improve your skills.

How that applies in the vibe coding world, I'm not sure. Maybe by getting better than average at vibe coding. (I'd be interested in your further thoughts on your last paragraph.)


Not for anything scheduled on a server. But if I could turn a 30-minute task into a local button press, sure, I'd often keep it to myself.

You have to decide whether your time is your own, or your employer's. The latter is a road to burnout. I always viewed myself as a one-man business, with my managers being my only customers. I decided for myself how best to keep them happy, while also keeping myself happy.

Another part of all this was estimates. Early in my career I just estimated my median expected time, which meant half the time my boss got mad at me. Later I gave estimates I was at least 90% likely to meet, and worked extra hours on the few occasions it took longer. Managers were happier because I hardly ever missed a deadline, and usually I had extra time, which I also kept to myself fairly often.

For the owner of the business, all this might not have been ideally profitable in the short term, though I think it worked out pretty well in the long term. It's a virtuous cycle if you spend some of your extra time productively. I ended up with a pretty easy job most of the time, but occasionally being the guy they called on to save a failing project, and then I was fresh enough to work like a maniac.


Some of it is fun and new, I'm spending a lot of time just making stuff I wanna make.

But regarding work produced for the marketplace, I think it is naive to think any productivity gains will ever produce more time on the beach for workers. The market is competitive. Some gains will be seized by capital, and others realized in the production of some combination of more stuff, cheaper stuff, or better stuff.


And yet, when I was a developer and the only way to automate things was by hand, I found that doing so could give me lots of extra free time.


There's definitely exceptions! People can make personal choices of course. Plus if you're early to something you can capture the gains before business and markets adapt.


> If I had access [to AI] back then, I'd probably just spend more time on the beach.

If AI were marketed like this it would not be appealing to employers. So of course AI marketing is wrapped in hustle culture. Gotta keep the worker bees busy.


I enjoy the fact that you were able to wedge Bukowski into this clusterfuck of technobabble , but the parallel being drawn between quality-writing and hitting buttons on the magic-elaboration-device ["ai"] is just... not there. Quality writing requires actual lived-experience, emotions, adventures, and a keen ability to grasp and clasp ends of an event-sequence like a beaded necklace or rosary; to present something cohesive and well-lived to someone who can imagine , provided ... the imagery and order-of-events are resonant.

Stylistically, I find Bukowski's "I know it / will" linebreak to be offensive to my aesthetic sensibilities as an excellent writer.


Summarybot (I feel silly for replying to a *bot*), that's a really good point, and I'd argue that creative writing and software development have a lot in common, especially now that English is the #1 programming language.

Nowadays when we can build software 50x faster, there are even greater benefits from spending time to speak with our prospects/customers.

This is the "working subconsciousness" take-away from Earnest Hemingway I wrote about here: https://galjot.si/what-ai-developers-could-learn-from-ernest...


Definitely put that "post" in the trash bin Bukowski was talking about. Took a perfectly fine idea from Hemingway and segued to a discussion about your bladder. Not a fan. But yes, Hemingway did say to always leave some ink in the quill. That is, to not deplete your wellspring of creativity to its last droplet, but to leave some in there and let it replenish itself naturally [overnight]. Yeah stepping away from the computer is a good idea, and also has nothing to do with being a good or effective writer. Your point about talking to customers as some sort of analogous moment to living life and being in the felt-sense , in contrast to writing , is really trying to fit a square peg in a round hole. It's okay for things to not be the same, to not be analogous, to evade parallellism. Managing the code-output of an LLM that is , by design , an endless elaboration device, is not the same as summoning from one's depths the diction that immortalizes otherwise fleeting scenes and images. Code is an instrument for modulating pixels, and while this can lead to new experiences, it is not the re-projection into the inner sensorium that good literature provides. You can sit in the passenger seat as a professional F1 racer takes you around the track, or you can change the oil on a car. That's the difference between great literature and great code.


"Wrong! The point of the story is the wife. Listen to your wife, she'll give you perspective. Meaning, you need a break. You have to take a bath or you'll get nowhere. There would be no order only chaos. Go home, Max, and you take a bath."


Your comment starts as a nice teaser… care to share more? When was that?

Judging by his writing, I get a sense that he became a bit more socially pleasant towards the end of his life?


Early 90's, I was checking out a dive bar in LA's Koreatown over lunch and noticed him at the bar. I happened to be reading one of his books a few night earlier, or I'd never have recognized the guy. It was one of those "welp, now or never" moments, and I got up and set next to him at the bar. After a glance and a "who the fuck are you?" I replied I was the idiot fan that was going to buy him drinks. His waving two fingers at the bartender was him indicating "okay" and we slowly started chatting. I ditched work for the afternoon, and had to call in sick the next, claiming my lunch was bad and made me sick. We smoked, this being when people could smoke indoors, and drank at that bar for hours. I think I slept in my car for a few hours too. He was a curmudgeon with a royal tongue. A life time memory, that afternoon. I think I was 25 then.


The takeaway message is you can be more on the beach and don’t have to ship 40k LoC everyday with your GStack. I like that.


I think it boils down to most of these folks don't have anything better to do. Or worse (the bucket I find myself in) this type of work is the most mentally stimulating thing I have, so I do it willfully at the expense of my wife and cats.

I'm still building the discipline to put the important stuff first!


By your own admission you are giving your work more import than your wife and cats. You are putting the important stuff (to you) first.


"There is way that seems right to a man, but the end thereof is death." Proverbs 14:12

By my own admission, I often place importance on the wrong things. I am building the discipline of putting the truly important things first.


When I was in college I took a class in modern poetry. The teacher showed us a film about Bukowski. Before the film, there was a trigger warning. "I must warn you," he said, "Charles Bukowski is an asshole."


My reaction to the title was "AI is learning enough from misogynistic assholes in its crawled data already, it doesn't need Bukowski's help."


Oh, yes. And I think he was proud of that.

> the best writers have said very little and the worst, far too much. > bag over his head in a bathtub full of water. what Hitler couldn’t do, he did to himself. happy journey.

Throughout reading the "Betting on the muse", I had plenty of "what an asshole" moments.


> If I had access [to AI] back then, I'd probably just spend more time on the beach.

This has been part of the critique of technology by primitivists for a while now; "labor saving" technology simply stops us from laboring on things we used to and we just move to laboring on other things on the newest level of abstraction with our freed up time / energy.

If society has uncurbed "greed", there can just be a constant "996 grind" on the cutting edge of whatever technological development currently exists.

> instead of forcing himself to write more slop (or ill words in his world) he stands up, moves away from his computer notebook and goes downstairs to his wife and 6 cats

or we could work on other projects, but yeah, take a break of some kind


> or we could work on other projects

spending time with family is the only other project that's worth it, besides the one that's paying the bills


Me: I like your solution, but could you unpack all those dense one-liners to make the code easier to follow?

Cursor: Do you wanna mess me up? Do you wanna screw up the works? You wanna blow my token sales in Europe?


> Why aren't tech folks sipping tequilas on the beach?

Because the environment mentioned earlier in the post - Silicon Valley - has absolutely nothing to offer but value creation. The people who rise up to leadership and success in that environment aren't particularly awesome human beings. The point isn't to make it better to be a human, it's to make all of the money.

All of the discussion about open models here of late offers a backdrop for what OpenAI was supposed to be versus what it turned out to be, and that offers a pretty good demonstration of the problem. Originally OpenAI was supposed to be a public benefit corporation that offered open models with a focus on ethics and safety. Their investors could expect "only" 100x return on their buy-in.

That, of course, didn't fill up the pockets of investors in SV to their liking, so the models became closed, the focus on safety and ethics went out the window, and the company became a typical for-profit corporation. The bet is now that they can hyperscale the deployment of closed models in a way that will generate an absolutely enormous amount of revenue and pay off the training and serving costs.

Meanwhile, Chinese developers of open models are taking the role that OpenAI was supposed to fulfill, with the obvious intent of undermining OpenAI and its ilk. They'll likely succeed, at least to some extent.

AI as it is now, at least in the major US labs based in SV, is almost purely for profit. The bet is huge and there can't be room for a penny to not be earned, for that tequila on a beach. It's an all-consuming philosophy in that region. If we want to see AI in the US have a sustainable path, you'll have to toss the people from that regional echo chamber. Maybe that'll happen if the monetary losses are big enough. Maybe not.


Come on, what would they need to learn that wasn't already "trained" by the LLMs ingestion of his works in the first instance??

sentences.en: It might be the future as more and more people find that the computer is such a magic thing: time-saver, charmer, energizer.”No one can say what he would have thought of AI for sure but I think he would have appreciated ability to reduce drudgery on this thoughts on factotum[1] work.1.
sentences.zh: 这可能是未来，因为越来越多的人发现计算机是一个神奇的东西：节省时间、迷人、充满活力。”没有人能确切地说出他对人工智能的看法，但我认为他会很感激能够减少杂工[1]工作中的苦差事。1。

sentences.en: Why yes, that is a cheesy reference to his book of the same name. ;) > On Christmas Day, 1990, Charles Bukowski received a Macintosh IIsi computer and a laser printer from his wife, Linda.
sentences.zh: 为什么是的，这是对他的同名书的俗气引用。 ;) > 1990 年圣诞节，Charles Bukowski 从他的妻子 Linda 那里收到了一台 Macintosh IIsi 电脑和一台激光打印机。

sentences.en: The computer utilized the 6.0.7 operating system and was installed with the MacWrite II word processing program.
sentences.zh: 该计算机使用6.0.7操作系统并安装了MacWrite II字处理程序。

sentences.en: By January 18 of the next year, the computer was up and running and so, after a brief period of fumbling and stumbling, was Bukowski.
sentences.zh: 到第二年 1 月 18 日，计算机已经启动并运行，经过短暂的摸索和绊倒后，布考斯基也完成了任务。

sentences.en: His output of poems doubled in 1991.Charles Bukowski, William Burroughs, and the Computer - https://realitystudio.org/bibliographic-bunker/charles-bukow... This cracked me up.
sentences.zh: 1991 年，他的诗歌产量翻了一番。查尔斯·布考斯基 (Charles Bukowski)、威廉·伯勒斯 (William Burroughs) 和计算机 - https://realitystudio.org/bibliography-bunker/charles-bukow... 这让我大笑。

sentences.en: I only used ~~one~~ two of his poems and enjoyed most of the others.
sentences.zh: 我只用过他的一首~~两首诗，其他的大部分诗我都很喜欢。

sentences.en: Betting on the Muse was $2.09 on Amazon, which is a good ROI, I think.
sentences.zh: 在亚马逊上押注 Muse 的价格为 2.09 美元，我认为这是一个不错的投资回报率。

sentences.en: Bukowski worked as a mailman.
sentences.zh: 布考斯基是一名邮递员。

sentences.en: I had that job too.
sentences.zh: 我也有那份工作。

sentences.en: It was an awesome job.
sentences.zh: 这是一项很棒的工作。

sentences.en: I got through like 9 hours of audiobooks a day.Only issue was nobody sends mail anymore -- the elderly, Christmas and spam -- so when there was no mail, you'd work an hour and then you'd only get paid one hour.
sentences.zh: 我每天听大约 9 个小时的有声读物。唯一的问题是没有人再发送邮件了——老人、圣诞节和垃圾邮件——所以当没有邮件时，你工作一个小时，然后你只能得到一个小时的工资。

sentences.en: So most people were students, or their spouse did the heavy lifting.Other than the pay, it was a great job though.
sentences.zh: 所以大多数人都是学生，或者他们的配偶承担着繁重的工作。除了工资之外，这是一份很棒的工作。

sentences.en: I worked in snowstorms (and regular storms!)
sentences.zh: 我在暴风雪中工作（还有普通的暴风雨！）

sentences.en: and in >37C (~100F) -- I got a big sombrero which looked a bit silly but did the job.Then I'd go home and work on genetic algorithms.
sentences.zh: 在 >37C (~100F) 的温度下——我得到了一顶大阔边帽，看起来有点傻，但确实有用。然后我回家研究遗传算法。

sentences.en: And then when the pay arrived at the end of the month -- 800 Euros (909 American), I had to wonder if I wasn't doing it backwards -- I should be getting paid to work on genetic algorithms all day, and then at the end of the day I should run up and down staircases for several hours for free.
sentences.zh: 然后，当月底收到工资时——800欧元（909美元），我不得不怀疑我是不是在倒退——我应该因为整天研究遗传算法而获得报酬，然后在一天结束时我应该免费在楼梯上跑上跑下几个小时。

sentences.en: All writing is difficult.
sentences.zh: 所有的写作都是困难的。

sentences.en: The most you can hope for is a day when it goes reasonably easily.
sentences.zh: 你最希望的就是有一天事情会变得相当轻松。

sentences.en: plumbers don't get plumbers block, and doctors don't get doctors block; why should writers be the only profession that gives a special name to the difficulty of working and then expects sympathy for it?—Philip Pullman > "Go into yourself.
sentences.zh: 水管工不会被水管工堵塞，医生不会被医生堵塞；为什么作家应该是唯一一个给工作的困难赋予特殊名称并期望得到同情的职业呢？——菲利普·普尔曼 > “深入你自己。

sentences.en: Find out the reason that commands you to write; see whether it has spread its roots into the very depths of your heart; confess to yourself whether you would have to die if you were forbidden to write.> This most of all: ask yourself in the most silent hour of your night: Must I write?
sentences.zh: 找出命令你写作的原因；看看它是否已经扎根到你的内心深处；向自己承认，如果你被禁止写作，你是否会死。 > 最重要的是：在夜晚最寂静的时刻问自己：我必须写作吗？

sentences.en: Dig into 1 yourself for a deep answer.
sentences.zh: 自己深入研究 1 以获得深刻的答案。

sentences.en: And if this answer rings out in assent, if you meet this solemn question with a strong, simple 'I must,' then build your life in accordance with this necessity..."--Rainer Maria RilkeMeanwhile Rilke gives no sympathy saying don't write because it is easy, hard, or your job, write because your existence demands it.I've found writing software for domains is agnostic; there isn't much difference between make a CRM for Real Estate or ERP for car mechanic shops.
sentences.zh: 如果这个答案听起来很同意，如果你用一个强烈而简单的“我必须”来面对这个庄严的问题，那么按照这种必要性来建立你的生活......”--Rainer Maria Rilke 同时，Rilke 没有表示同情，他说不要因为它容易、困难或你的工作而写作，而是因为你的存在需要它而写作。我发现为领域编写软件是不可知的；为房地产开发 CRM 或为房地产开发 ERP 之间没有太大区别汽车修理店。

sentences.en: It is curious that I know one person who is as passionate about the event ticket industry as Rilke is about writing -- they would rather die than not scalp tickets.I would have to read `Letters to a Young Poet again`.
sentences.zh: 奇怪的是，我认识一个像里尔克对写作一样热衷于活动门票行业的人——他们宁愿死也不愿不抢票。我得再读一遍《给一位年轻诗人的信》。

sentences.en: Rilke addresses the difference between being an artist (Rilke a Poet apprenticed under Rodin to learn not sculpture but guidance to live as an artist) and entering a structured profession.
sentences.zh: 里尔克谈到了成为一名艺术家（里尔克是一位诗人，在罗丹的指导下学习的不是雕塑，而是指导如何作为艺术家生活）和进入结构化职业之间的区别。

sentences.en: Beautiful.Charles Bukowski said something similar…> /…/ no baby, if you’re going to create you’re going to create whether you work 16 hours a day in a coal mine or you’re going to create in a small room with 3 children while you’re on welfare, you’re going to create with part of your mind and your body blown away, you’re going to create blind crippled demented, you’re going to create with a cat crawling up your back while the whole city trembles in earthquake, bombardment, flood and fire.
sentences.zh: 美丽。查尔斯·布考斯基说过类似的话…> /…/不，宝贝，如果你要创造，你就要创造，无论你每天在煤矿工作 16 个小时，还是在领取福利金的情况下，在一个带着 3 个孩子的小房间里创造，你要在你的一部分思想和身体被吹走的情况下进行创造，你要创造一个失明的、残废的、精神错乱的人，你要在一只猫在你背上爬的时候，而整个城市都在创造。在地震、轰炸、洪水和火灾中颤抖。

sentences.en: baby, air and light and time and space have nothing to do with it and don’t create anything except maybe a longer life to find new excuses for.
sentences.zh: 宝贝，空气、光、时间和空间都与它无关，除了可能为更长的生命找到新的借口之外，不会创造任何东西。

sentences.en: I said last year, "if I'd known I was going to be homeless for this long, I would have just kept working on my game the whole time."It seemed logical, at the time, to postpone such frivolous affairs until life was more orderly.
sentences.zh: 我去年说过，“如果我知道自己会无家可归这么久，我就会一直专注于我的比赛。”当时，推迟这些琐碎的事情直到生活变得更加有序，似乎是合乎逻辑的。

sentences.en: But it sure didn't help speed things along.On another note, I have also heard it said that one must suffer for one's art, but I haven't found much correlation personally between suffering and art...
sentences.zh: 但这确实无助于加快事情的进展。另一方面，我也听人说，一个人必须为自己的艺术而受苦，但我个人并没有发现苦难和艺术之间有太大的关联……

sentences.en: except perhaps to the degree that JavaScript is involved!
sentences.zh: 除非涉及 JavaScript 的程度！

sentences.en: A while back I started a substack and diligently posted every day, for about a month.The first few posts had some actual substance (a kind of backlog I suppose), but eventually I realized that I was just posting because I had decided to post and I didn't actually have anything left to say.So I just stopped posting.
sentences.zh: 不久前，我开始了一个子堆栈，每天都在努力发布，持续了大约一个月。前几篇帖子有一些实际内容（我想是一种积压），但最终我意识到我只是在发帖，因为我已经决定发帖，而我实际上没有什么可说的。所以我就停止发帖了。

sentences.en: I guess it'll probably be a few more years until the next one :)(Gosh, just imagine if YouTube operated on this principle...)
sentences.zh: 我想下一个可能还需要几年的时间:)（天哪，想象一下 YouTube 是否按照这个原则运作......）

sentences.en: “. . .a lonely room, with a cup of coffee, facing a blank piece of paper.”Wouk elaborated on that predicament.
sentences.zh: “……一个孤独的房间，一杯咖啡，面对一张白纸。”沃克详细阐述了这个困境。

sentences.en: He said that writer William Faulkner was asked, ‘Mr. Faulkner, do you write on inspiration or do you write on a schedule?’
sentences.zh: 他说作家威廉·福克纳被问到，“先生。”福克纳，你是根据灵感写作还是按时间表写作？

sentences.en: Faulkner replied.
sentences.zh: 福克纳回答道。

sentences.en: ‘Well, of course I write on inspiration.
sentences.zh: “嗯，我当然是根据灵感来写作的。

sentences.en: Fortunately, it strikes every morning at a quarter past nine.’https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/30/inspire-nine/ I'm not a plumber, but I'm in the trades, and we absolutely get a "block", but we grind through it. >Why aren't we spending more time on the beach.I think this comes down to getting paid per effort invested (measured in time) vs getting paid for the result.If the average person were self-employed and received income proportional to their economic output, then they would be rewarded for working faster, instead of punished.If they increased their productivity, by means of technology, they could then simply choose to work fewer hours.[0]I noticed this before AI.
sentences.zh: 幸运的是，它每天早上九点一刻敲响。’https://quoteinvestigator.com/2013/10/30/inspire-nine/ 我不是水管工，但我从事行业，我们绝对会遇到“障碍”，但我们会努力克服它。 >为什么我们不在海滩上花更多的时间。我认为这归结为按投入的努力（以时间衡量）获得报酬与按结果获得报酬。如果普通人是个体经营者，收入与他们的经济产出成正比，那么他们会因为工作更快而获得奖励，而不是受到惩罚。如果他们通过技术提高生产力，那么他们可以简单地选择减少工作时间。[0]我在人工智能出现之前就注意到了这一点。

sentences.en: If someone does the same job twice as fast, do they deserve half as much compensation?What if they find a way to automate an entire process?
sentences.zh: 如果某人以两倍的速度完成同样的工作，他们是否应该得到一半的报酬？如果他们找到一种方法来自动化整个流程怎么办？

sentences.en: What if they replace months of "manual labor" (tedious refactoring) with a perl script that produces the same result, deterministically?A friend of mine once automated a woman's entire job away.
sentences.zh: 如果他们用 Perl 脚本取代数月的“体力劳动”（繁琐的重构），并确定性地产生相同的结果，会怎么样？我的一个朋友曾经自动化了一位女性的整个工作。

sentences.en: He thought he was doing her a favour, freeing her from the drudgery, so she could focus on the other parts of the job.
sentences.zh: 他认为他是在帮她一个忙，让她摆脱苦差事，这样她就可以专注于工作的其他部分。

sentences.en: She wasn't so happy, when she revealed to him, that there weren't any.---[0] But most people aren't in such a position, and have to stay the required number of hours regardless of how much has been achieved.
sentences.zh: 当她向他透露没有的时候，她不太高兴。---[0] 但大多数人并没有处于这样的境地，无论取得了多少成就，都必须坚持规定的时间。

sentences.en: And I'm increasingly hearing reports of some kind of burnout resulting from being expected to keep up with machines that work a thousand times faster than you.And that's now...
sentences.zh: 我越来越多地听到有关某种倦怠的报道，因为人们期望跟上比你工作速度快一千倍的机器。而现在......

sentences.en: Just wait until the big providers switch to Cerebras in a week or two!(Though at that token speed, the silver lining is the work becomes interactive again, so if you use it correctly, your mental model does not desynchronize from the codebase, i.e. you don't need to spend extra time later catching up.
sentences.zh: 只需等到大型提供商在一两周内转向 Cerebras 即可！（虽然以这种象征性的速度，一线希望是工作再次变得交互式，所以如果你正确使用它，你的心智模型不会与代码库不同步，即你不需要花费额外的时间来追赶。

sentences.en: But that deserves its own thread, I think :) Your friend could have still done the woman a favor, if he shared the automation with her privately, instead of with their employer.Doing things like this for yourself is how you make automation work for you instead of against you.
sentences.zh: 但这值得有自己的主题，我认为:)如果你的朋友私下与她而不是与他们的雇主分享自动化，他仍然可以帮那个女人一个忙。为自己做这样的事情就是让自动化为你工作而不是对你不利。

sentences.en: Then you can take some of your extra time to automate even more.
sentences.zh: 然后您可以花一些额外的时间来实现更多自动化。

sentences.en: Or, if you're a dev, to clean up code so it's easier to work on later, or to improve your skills.How that applies in the vibe coding world, I'm not sure.
sentences.zh: 或者，如果您是开发人员，则可以清理代码，以便以后更轻松地工作，或者提高您的技能。我不确定这如何应用于氛围编码世界。

sentences.en: Maybe by getting better than average at vibe coding.
sentences.zh: 也许是通过在氛围编码方面比平均水平更好。

sentences.en: (I'd be interested in your further thoughts on your last paragraph.)
sentences.zh: （我对你对最后一段的进一步想法感兴趣。）

sentences.en: Not for anything scheduled on a server.
sentences.zh: 不适用于服务器上安排的任何内容。

sentences.en: But if I could turn a 30-minute task into a local button press, sure, I'd often keep it to myself.You have to decide whether your time is your own, or your employer's.
sentences.zh: 但是，如果我可以将 30 分钟的任务变成按本地按钮，当然，我通常会把它留给自己。你必须决定你的时间是属于你自己的，还是属于你雇主的。

sentences.en: The latter is a road to burnout.
sentences.zh: 后者是一条通往倦怠之路。

sentences.en: I always viewed myself as a one-man business, with my managers being my only customers.
sentences.zh: 我一直将自己视为一个人的企业，我的经理是我唯一的客户。

sentences.en: I decided for myself how best to keep them happy, while also keeping myself happy.Another part of all this was estimates.
sentences.zh: 我自己决定如何最好地让他们开心，同时也让自己开心。这一切的另一部分是估计。

sentences.en: Early in my career I just estimated my median expected time, which meant half the time my boss got mad at me.
sentences.zh: 在我职业生涯的早期，我只是估计了我的平均预期时间，这意味着我的老板有一半的时间对我生气。

sentences.en: Later I gave estimates I was at least 90% likely to meet, and worked extra hours on the few occasions it took longer.
sentences.zh: 后来我估计我至少有 90% 的可能会见，并在少数需要更长时间的情况下加班。

sentences.en: Managers were happier because I hardly ever missed a deadline, and usually I had extra time, which I also kept to myself fairly often.For the owner of the business, all this might not have been ideally profitable in the short term, though I think it worked out pretty well in the long term.
sentences.zh: 经理们更高兴，因为我几乎没有错过最后期限，而且通常我有额外的时间，而且我也经常把这些时间留给自己。 对于企业主来说，所有这些在短期内可能不会带来理想的盈利，尽管我认为从长远来看效果很好。

sentences.en: It's a virtuous cycle if you spend some of your extra time productively.
sentences.zh: 如果你有效地利用一些额外的时间，这就是一个良性循环。

sentences.en: I ended up with a pretty easy job most of the time, but occasionally being the guy they called on to save a failing project, and then I was fresh enough to work like a maniac.
sentences.zh: 大多数时候我都得到了一份相当轻松的工作，但偶尔也会成为他们呼吁挽救失败项目的人，然后我就有足够的新鲜感像疯子一样工作。

sentences.en: Some of it is fun and new, I'm spending a lot of time just making stuff I wanna make.But regarding work produced for the marketplace, I think it is naive to think any productivity gains will ever produce more time on the beach for workers.
sentences.zh: 其中一些很有趣而且很新，我花了很多时间只是制作我想做的东西。但是对于为市场制作的作品，我认为认为任何生产力的提高都会为工人带来更多在海滩上的时间的想法是天真的。

sentences.en: The market is competitive.
sentences.zh: 市场竞争激烈。

sentences.en: Some gains will be seized by capital, and others realized in the production of some combination of more stuff, cheaper stuff, or better stuff.
sentences.zh: 一些收益将被资本攫取，而另一些收益则通过生产更多的东西、更便宜的东西或更好的东西的某种组合来实现。

sentences.en: And yet, when I was a developer and the only way to automate things was by hand, I found that doing so could give me lots of extra free time.
sentences.zh: 然而，当我还是一名开发人员时，实现自动化的唯一方法是手动，我发现这样做可以给我带来很多额外的空闲时间。

sentences.en: There's definitely exceptions!
sentences.zh: 肯定有例外！

sentences.en: People can make personal choices of course.
sentences.zh: 人们当然可以做出个人选择。

sentences.en: Plus if you're early to something you can capture the gains before business and markets adapt. > If I had access [to AI] back then, I'd probably just spend more time on the beach.If AI were marketed like this it would not be appealing to employers.
sentences.zh: 另外，如果您尽早采取行动，您可以在业务和市场适应之前获得收益。 > 如果我当时能够接触到人工智能，我可能会花更多时间在海滩上。如果人工智能像这样营销，它不会对雇主有吸引力。

sentences.en: So of course AI marketing is wrapped in hustle culture.
sentences.zh: 因此，人工智能营销当然是包含在喧嚣文化中的。

sentences.en: Gotta keep the worker bees busy.
sentences.zh: 得让工蜂忙碌起来。

sentences.en: I enjoy the fact that you were able to wedge Bukowski into this clusterfuck of technobabble , but the parallel being drawn between quality-writing and hitting buttons on the magic-elaboration-device ["ai"] is just...
sentences.zh: 我很高兴你能够把布考斯基塞进这堆技术废话中，但是高质量写作和点击魔法阐述设备 [“ai”] 上的按钮之间的相似之处只是......

sentences.en: not there.
sentences.zh: 不在那里。

sentences.en: Quality writing requires actual lived-experience, emotions, adventures, and a keen ability to grasp and clasp ends of an event-sequence like a beaded necklace or rosary; to present something cohesive and well-lived to someone who can imagine , provided ...
sentences.zh: 高质量的写作需要真实的生活经历、情感、冒险，以及敏锐的能力来抓住和抓住事件序列的末端，就像串珠项链或念珠一样；向有想象力的人呈现一些有凝聚力和美好生活的东西，前提是......

sentences.en: the imagery and order-of-events are resonant.Stylistically, I find Bukowski's "I know it / will" linebreak to be offensive to my aesthetic sensibilities as an excellent writer.
sentences.zh: 从风格上来说，我发现布考斯基的“我知道/会”的台词冒犯了我作为一名优秀作家的审美感受。

blocks.html_en:
Creatives have always found inspiration from what they consume (AI has nothing to do with it). My partner writes, and eventually gets to the point where she has to take a break from plotting and writing and watch tv shows or read books. When she says she needs to refill her well, I know she's about to want to watch tv shows again for a little bit.

I design games. I can't even count the number of times something someone said, or a game I've played or watched a review of, has sparked an idea for new game, especially a board game (which most of the time doesn't work out once it gets in front of players, but that's okay). It's probably been over a hundred times by now.

People love highlighting quotes from poems and stories that they find inspirational for their own lives somehow. You want to know how I know? Kindle used to tell me, with saying how many other people highlighted a specific passage (it might still do that, but I mostly listen to audiobooks right now, so of course I won't see them). Also social media is flooded with people sharing quotes from various books or poems or sayings from people.

That's all this is.

But because it's said by someone who works with A.I. and thus is thinking about the quote with that frame of reference, you had to twist it into some anti-A.I. sentiment, implying that he's doing something perverted or not normal by daring to find inspiration in a quote.

blocks.html_en:
Creatives have always found inspiration from what they consume (AI has nothing to do with it). My partner writes, and eventually gets to the point where she has to take a break from plotting and writing and watch tv shows or read books. When she says she needs to refill her well, I know she's about to want to watch tv shows again for a little bit.

I design games. I can't even count the number of times something someone said, or a game I've played or watched a review of, has sparked an idea for new game, especially a board game (which most of the time doesn't work out once it gets in front of players, but that's okay). It's probably been over a hundred times by now.

People love highlighting quotes from poems and stories that they find inspirational for their own lives somehow. You want to know how I know? Kindle used to tell me, with saying how many other people highlighted a specific passage (it might still do that, but I mostly listen to audiobooks right now, so of course I won't see them). Also social media is flooded with people sharing quotes from various books or poems or sayings from people.

That's all this is.

But because it's said by someone who works with A.I. and thus is thinking about the quote with that frame of reference, you had to twist it into some anti-A.I. sentiment, implying that he's doing something perverted or not normal by daring to find inspiration in a quote.

Bukowski worked as a mailman. I had that job too. It was an awesome job. I got through like 9 hours of audiobooks a day.

Only issue was nobody sends mail anymore -- the elderly, Christmas and spam -- so when there was no mail, you'd work an hour and then you'd only get paid one hour. So most people were students, or their spouse did the heavy lifting.

Other than the pay, it was a great job though. I worked in snowstorms (and regular storms!) and in >37C (~100F) -- I got a big sombrero which looked a bit silly but did the job.

Then I'd go home and work on genetic algorithms. And then when the pay arrived at the end of the month -- 800 Euros (909 American), I had to wonder if I wasn't doing it backwards -- I should be getting paid to work on genetic algorithms all day, and then at the end of the day I should run up and down staircases for several hours for free.

Only issue was nobody sends mail anymore -- the elderly, Christmas and spam -- so when there was no mail, you'd work an hour and then you'd only get paid one hour. So most people were students, or their spouse did the heavy lifting.

Other than the pay, it was a great job though. I worked in snowstorms (and regular storms!) and in >37C (~100F) -- I got a big sombrero which looked a bit silly but did the job.

Then I'd go home and work on genetic algorithms. And then when the pay arrived at the end of the month -- 800 Euros (909 American), I had to wonder if I wasn't doing it backwards -- I should be getting paid to work on genetic algorithms all day, and then at the end of the day I should run up and down staircases for several hours for free.

blocks.html_en:
> "Go into yourself. Find out the reason that commands you to write; see whether it has spread its roots into the very depths of your heart; confess to yourself whether you would have to die if you were forbidden to write.

> This most of all: ask yourself in the most silent hour of your night: Must I write? Dig into 1 yourself for a deep answer. And if this answer rings out in assent, if you meet this solemn question with a strong, simple 'I must,' then build your life in accordance with this necessity..."

--Rainer Maria Rilke

Meanwhile Rilke gives no sympathy saying don't write because it is easy, hard, or your job, write because your existence demands it.

I've found writing software for domains is agnostic; there isn't much difference between make a CRM for Real Estate or ERP for car mechanic shops. It is curious that I know one person who is as passionate about the event ticket industry as Rilke is about writing -- they would rather die than not scalp tickets.

I would have to read `Letters to a Young Poet again`. Rilke addresses the difference between being an artist (Rilke a Poet apprenticed under Rodin to learn not sculpture but guidance to live as an artist) and entering a structured profession.

A while back I started a substack and diligently posted every day, for about a month.

The first few posts had some actual substance (a kind of backlog I suppose), but eventually I realized that I was just posting because I had decided to post and I didn't actually have anything left to say.

So I just stopped posting. I guess it'll probably be a few more years until the next one :)

(Gosh, just imagine if YouTube operated on this principle...)

blocks.html_en:
>Why aren't we spending more time on the beach.

I think this comes down to getting paid per effort invested (measured in time) vs getting paid for the result.

If the average person were self-employed and received income proportional to their economic output, then they would be rewarded for working faster, instead of punished.

If they increased their productivity, by means of technology, they could then simply choose to work fewer hours.[0]

I noticed this before AI. If someone does the same job twice as fast, do they deserve half as much compensation?

What if they find a way to automate an entire process? What if they replace months of "manual labor" (tedious refactoring) with a perl script that produces the same result, deterministically?

A friend of mine once automated a woman's entire job away. He thought he was doing her a favour, freeing her from the drudgery, so she could focus on the other parts of the job. She wasn't so happy, when she revealed to him, that there weren't any.

---

[0] But most people aren't in such a position, and have to stay the required number of hours regardless of how much has been achieved. And I'm increasingly hearing reports of some kind of burnout resulting from being expected to keep up with machines that work a thousand times faster than you.

And that's now... Just wait until the big providers switch to Cerebras in a week or two!

(Though at that token speed, the silver lining is the work becomes interactive again, so if you use it correctly, your mental model does not desynchronize from the codebase, i.e. you don't need to spend extra time later catching up. But that deserves its own thread, I think :)

blocks.html_en:
Not for anything scheduled on a server. But if I could turn a 30-minute task into a local button press, sure, I'd often keep it to myself.

You have to decide whether your time is your own, or your employer's. The latter is a road to burnout. I always viewed myself as a one-man business, with my managers being my only customers. I decided for myself how best to keep them happy, while also keeping myself happy.

Another part of all this was estimates. Early in my career I just estimated my median expected time, which meant half the time my boss got mad at me. Later I gave estimates I was at least 90% likely to meet, and worked extra hours on the few occasions it took longer. Managers were happier because I hardly ever missed a deadline, and usually I had extra time, which I also kept to myself fairly often.

For the owner of the business, all this might not have been ideally profitable in the short term, though I think it worked out pretty well in the long term. It's a virtuous cycle if you spend some of your extra time productively. I ended up with a pretty easy job most of the time, but occasionally being the guy they called on to save a failing project, and then I was fresh enough to work like a maniac.

I enjoy the fact that you were able to wedge Bukowski into this clusterfuck of technobabble , but the parallel being drawn between quality-writing and hitting buttons on the magic-elaboration-device ["ai"] is just... not there. Stylistically, I find Bukowski's "I know it / will" linebreak to be offensive to my aesthetic sensibilities as an excellent writer.

blocks.html_en: Definitely put that "post" in the trash bin Bukowski was talking about. Took a perfectly fine idea from Hemingway and segued to a discussion about your bladder. Not a fan. But yes, Hemingway did say to always leave some ink in the quill. That is, to not deplete your wellspring of creativity to its last droplet, but to leave some in there and let it replenish itself naturally [overnight]. Yeah stepping away from the computer is a good idea, and also has nothing to do with being a good or effective writer. Your point about talking to customers as some sort of analogous moment to living life and being in the felt-sense , in contrast to writing , is really trying to fit a square peg in a round hole. It's okay for things to not be the same, to not be analogous, to evade parallellism. Managing the code-output of an LLM that is , by design , an endless elaboration device, is not the same as summoning from one's depths the diction that immortalizes otherwise fleeting scenes and images. Code is an instrument for modulating pixels, and while this can lead to new experiences, it is not the re-projection into the inner sensorium that good literature provides. You can sit in the passenger seat as a professional F1 racer takes you around the track, or you can change the oil on a car. That's the difference between great literature and great code.

That is, to not deplete your wellspring of creativity to its last droplet, but to leave some in there and let it replenish itself naturally [overnight]. Yeah stepping away from the computer is a good idea, and also has nothing to do with being a good or effective writer. Your point about talking to customers as some sort of analogous moment to living life and being in the felt-sense , in contrast to writing , is really trying to fit a square peg in a round hole. It's okay for things to not be the same, to not be analogous, to evade parallellism. Managing the code-output of an LLM that is , by design , an endless elaboration device, is not the same as summoning from one's depths the diction that immortalizes otherwise fleeting scenes and images. Code is an instrument for modulating pixels, and while this can lead to new experiences, it is not the re-projection into the inner sensorium that good literature provides. You can sit in the passenger seat as a professional F1 racer takes you around the track, or you can change the oil on a car. That's the difference between great literature and great code.

blocks.html_en: Early 90's, I was checking out a dive bar in LA's Koreatown over lunch and noticed him at the bar. I happened to be reading one of his books a few night earlier, or I'd never have recognized the guy. It was one of those "welp, now or never" moments, and I got up and set next to him at the bar. After a glance and a "who the fuck are you?" I replied I was the idiot fan that was going to buy him drinks. His waving two fingers at the bartender was him indicating "okay" and we slowly started chatting. I ditched work for the afternoon, and had to call in sick the next, claiming my lunch was bad and made me sick. We smoked, this being when people could smoke indoors, and drank at that bar for hours. I think I slept in my car for a few hours too. He was a curmudgeon with a royal tongue. A life time memory, that afternoon. I think I was 25 then.

> Why aren't tech folks sipping tequilas on the beach?

Because the environment mentioned earlier in the post - Silicon Valley - has absolutely nothing to offer but value creation. The people who rise up to leadership and success in that environment aren't particularly awesome human beings. The point isn't to make it better to be a human, it's to make all of the money.

All of the discussion about open models here of late offers a backdrop for what OpenAI was supposed to be versus what it turned out to be, and that offers a pretty good demonstration of the problem. Originally OpenAI was supposed to be a public benefit corporation that offered open models with a focus on ethics and safety. Their investors could expect "only" 100x return on their buy-in.

That, of course, didn't fill up the pockets of investors in SV to their liking, so the models became closed, the focus on safety and ethics went out the window, and the company became a typical for-profit corporation. The bet is now that they can hyperscale the deployment of closed models in a way that will generate an absolutely enormous amount of revenue and pay off the training and serving costs.

Meanwhile, Chinese developers of open models are taking the role that OpenAI was supposed to fulfill, with the obvious intent of undermining OpenAI and its ilk. They'll likely succeed, at least to some extent.

AI as it is now, at least in the major US labs based in SV, is almost purely for profit. The bet is huge and there can't be room for a penny to not be earned, for that tequila on a beach. It's an all-consuming philosophy in that region. If we want to see AI in the US have a sustainable path, you'll have to toss the people from that regional echo chamber. Maybe that'll happen if the monetary losses are big enough. Maybe not.
